Rufous-breasted antthrush (Formicarius rufipectus) neonates emerge from eggs at a remarkably advanced state compared to many passerines. Field observations indicate that the incubation period lasts approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days] when eggs are maintained at an average temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], a value derived from congeners due to the difficulty of directly monitoring nests in dense understory. At hatching, the initial wet weight of the altricial nestling is a modest 6.8 grams [Ww0 = 6.8 grams], placing them among the lighter-bodied antthrush species at this critical life stage. This low neonatal mass necessitates intense parental provisioning during the early nestling phase, as the chicks must rapidly acquire the energy reserves required for feather development and thermoregulation before they can fledge into the humid, shaded environment of the Andean cloud forest they inhabit.

Under the thermal conditions typical of an active adult's resting metabolism, approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the developmental schedule of Formicarius rufipectus unfolds in a precise sequence. The fledging period, representing the time from hatching to the achievement of first flight, is estimated at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching], a duration that aligns closely with data from the closely related Formicarius analis at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Following this milestone, the young birds enter a prolonged period of nutritional dependence on their parents. The onset of sexual maturation occurs considerably later, with puberty being reached at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching], marking the point at which the gonads begin to develop and the individual enters the sub-adult phase of its life history at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Comparative physiological studies have provided key insights into the energetic demands of this secretive forest floor specialist. The basal metabolic rate (BMR), measured under standard resting conditions at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], has been recorded at 132.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 132.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value represents the maximum metabolic output for a non-active individual and serves as a critical benchmark for understanding the species' daily energy requirements. These metabolic data are particularly relevant given the bird's insectivorous diet and its constant activity in the cool, shaded microhabitats of the lower montane forest, where prey capture and territory defense demand substantial aerobic capacity.

For females, the ultimate wet body mass achieved upon reaching full adult size is 74.7 grams [Wwi = 74.7 grams]. This adult mass, which is considerably greater than the initial hatchling weight, is attained through a sustained period of growth and resource acquisition that extends well beyond the fledging stage. The species’ annual reproductive output is defined by the combination of clutch size and breeding frequency. Females typically produce a single clutch of 2 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nesting attempt], and available data, again informed by studies on Formicarius analis, suggest that they successfully raise one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year], reflecting the constraints imposed by a relatively short breeding season in high-altitude tropical environments.

The maximum documented lifespan for Formicarius rufipectus under the thermal conditions of its active metabolism, 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 10.1 years [am = approximately 10.1 years], a longevity that places it amongst the longer-lived members of its genus. This substantial lifespan is accompanied by a delayed onset of full reproductive activity; the time from birth to the first successful brood is estimated at about 1.4 years after hatching [tR = about 1.4 years after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This deferred reproductive effort is characteristic of species that invest heavily in the survival of each individual offspring and that occupy stable, low-variance environments. The combination of a protracted pre-reproductive period, a single annual brood, and a moderate clutch size underscores a life-history strategy centered on adult persistence rather than high fecundity.
